title: Robe (Kosode) with Pine, Ivy, Chrysanthemums, and River
medium: Crepe silk with resist-dyeing and silk- and metallic-thread embroidery

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Purchase, Anonymous Gift, 2018

altText: A Japanese silk robe patterned with pine, ivy, chrysanthemums and a river, with some of the plants picked out in embroidery that includes shiny metallic thread.

context: A kosode, the small-sleeved robe from which the kimono developed, made in Japan in the mid-19th century. It is crepe silk decorated with resist-dyeing and embroidery in silk and metallic thread. Its design combines pine, ivy, chrysanthemums, and a river.

descriptions.k: This silk robe has a garden on it! Pine trees, ivy leaves, and flowers grow beside a river. Some parts are stitched with shiny thread. Where do you think the water is? Can you find a flower?
descriptions.g12: This silk robe from Japan is covered with a design of pine, ivy, chrysanthemum flowers, and a river. Some parts were dyed and some were sewn with thread, including shiny metal thread. It is like a garden you can wear. Which plant would you look at first?
descriptions.g35: This kosode, made in Japan in the mid-1800s, turns a robe into a landscape. Pine, ivy, chrysanthemums, and a river are combined in one design. The maker used resist-dyeing, which keeps dye out of chosen areas, and added embroidery with silk and metallic thread that catches the light. Why might a designer want parts of the robe to sparkle? How do the plants and river fit together?
descriptions.g68: This mid-19th century kosode combines dyeing and embroidery, two ways of putting images on cloth. Resist-dyeing creates broad areas, while silk and metallic embroidery adds raised detail and shine. The mix of pine, ivy, chrysanthemums, and a river suggests a seasonal landscape. Designs like these sometimes echo poetry or stories, though a specific meaning would need evidence. How do texture and shimmer change the way you read the design?
descriptions.g910: The robe works as a large pictorial surface in which dyeing sets the ground and embroidery adds relief and sparkle. Pine, ivy, chrysanthemums, and a river combine nature motifs common in Edo-period design, and some such combinations may allude to poetry or literature, although this is not something the image alone proves. Consider how metallic thread shifts with light and movement, and how the composition might wrap a moving body rather than hang flat on a wall.
descriptions.g1112: This kosode shows the late Edo-period appetite for rich surface: resist-dyed silk crepe supplemented by silk and metallic-thread embroidery. Its imagery of pine, ivy, chrysanthemums, and a river belongs to a vocabulary of nature motifs that could carry seasonal, literary, or auspicious associations, but attributing one meaning requires evidence we may not have. The reflective thread also complicates photography and display, since the work changes with light and movement. How do material, motif, and viewing conditions shape our reading?

teacherNote.context: A mid-19th century kosode in crepe silk with resist-dyeing and embroidery in silk and metallic thread, from the Edo period. The kosode is the forerunner of the modern kimono.
directions: Have students design a robe motif set that tells a seasonal story, then explain which parts would be dyed and which stitched.
Use a flashlight to show how shiny thread changes with light, then discuss how photographs capture only one view.
Compare with the other robes in the archive to see how designers handle seasons and symbols.
